title: Have you ever seen a Zugzwang/Windmill?
originalTitle: Have you ever seen a Zugzwang/Windmill? #chess #puzzle #zugzwang
reviewNotes: Complete seven-piece later pawn-release position reconstructed after forced ...h6 across 54–56-second boards; bridge separately saved. Kc2 is the only winning move, forcing ...hxg5/hxg5/h4, then the source promotion race reaches actual Qg7 mate after ...h1=Q. Either immediate g6 or gxh6 is actual stalemate. Earlier eight-piece waiting choice and introductory examples remain outside proof.
transcript: Have you ever seen a zuklong windmill? Let me explain. You see, in chess, a windmill is a check that you can repeat over and over again, allowing you to win a whole bunch of pieces. And zukswang happens when the best move on the board would be to not move any piece whatsoever. Like in this case, the king would want to stay in front of the pawn. But because of the rules of the game, it is forced to leave his position and white will be able to get a queen. So it makes sense that a windmill zukwang is a combination of the two. In this position, the only winning move for white is to play king C1, blocking the black king in the corner and forcing black to move one of his pawns instead. But now, we don't want to take this pawn because this would allow H5, putting us in Zukwang because now we either have to let the black king out of his cage, allowing him to get a queen, drawing the game, or we move a pawn and stalemate. So the solution is actually to repeat the zuk swang, forcing black to keep moving the pawns until we can finally capture the g5 pawn like this allowing black to have some moves to play. But once we get a queen, we can now play this checkmate.
